```{r include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
```

### Background

On May 17th, 2026 I woke up to some surprising heat and humidity. April had some pretty cold days so this sudden change was unexpected. I decided to look at the weather history and see if I could find patterns.

### Data Acquisition

I looked for datasets online that could tell me the previous 30 years of daily highs for temperature in Boston. My instinct was that May had not always been this hot, and I wanted to test this idea.

After failing to find ready to use data, I came accross a website called wunderground.com that could at least tell me the high temperatures on any date I wanted. So I just read the temperatures and manually entered them into R.

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)

temp <- c(80, 69, 66, 75, 77, 69, 68, 75, 91, 70, 80, 75, 69, 71, 50, 75, 64, 74, 52, 70, 66, 70, 53, 74, 61, 70, 73, 68, 61, 67, 57)


(x <- tibble(temp = rev(temp), year = 1995:2025))
```

Not sure why I omitted 2026, but that's how it goes sometimes.

### Graphing and Modeling

Let's take a look at the raw data:

```{r}
x %>%
  ggplot(aes(year, temp)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1996, 2025, 4))
```

Clearly there is an upwards trend:

```{r}
x %>%
  ggplot(aes(year, temp)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1996, 2025, 4))
```

Not bad. And we even get some confidence intervals for the predicted mean. They get wider near the edges of the data, seemingly because there is less local information there. You can see that the width of this interval is symmetric about the center of the data.

My gut tells me to get rid of those spikes as they are confusing and difficult to reason with. We can extract the trend using a different type of model, one much more common in time series: a moving average!


```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
x %>%
  mutate(
    lag0 = temp,
    lag1 = lag(temp),
    lag2 = lag(temp, 2),
    lead1 = lead(temp),
    lead2 = lead(temp, 2)
  ) %>%
  na.omit() %>%
  gather(,,lag0:lead2) %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  transmute(year, temp, ma_5 = mean(value)) %>%
  gather("series", "value", -year) %>%
  ggplot(aes(year, value, color = series)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1996, 2025, 4))
```

Much more interesting. The moving average with a window of width 5 is an intuitive way to smooth a times series. As we know, time welcomes change, leading to sizable variance (spikes). The moving average takes data and filters out noise so that we can see the underlying trend.

### Model Interpretations

The resulting model and graph do a good job of explaining things on their own. Here's what I find most interesting:

1) There is a clear leap in the highs for May 17th starting from 2012 and peaking in 2016
2) Temperatures appear rather stable from 1997 to 2012
3) Temperatures seem to slope down after the 2016 peak
4) Temperatures appear to reach a new, higher level post 2012, albeit less stable than before

The apparent stability pre-2012 leading into such a great leap suggests that this is more than random. My personal comment is that this is due to the end of the Mayan calendar. Jokes aside, I do believe that this may have something to do with the explosion of smartphones and a new internet. By the year 2016, just about everyone became integrated into a heavily commercialized online world. Advertisers could not only deliver ads right into people's hands, but the data they collected from apps and websites made ads more effective. More buying and selling throttled industry and manufacturing, leading to global warming.

The post-2016 decline could be due to an intervention that was made once this heating trend was recognized. After all, much of this is in humanity's control. What I find interesting is that the trend begins to increase again after the downwards slope, suggesting that the intervention was only a temporary solution. However, this final increase in the model is not unlike previous deviations seen in the moving average. The size of the deviation isn't very large.

Overall, the post-2012 temperatures look rather unstable.

### Model Considerations and Simulation

Averaging over time is a clean, simple way to extract the trend without introducing bias. It is very easy for human intervention and model tuning to "confirm" one's bias. Our choice of models (ordinary least squares and moving average) were chosen after looking at the data. However, it is fair to say that these are baseline models that would have been invoked regardless of any patterns witnessed in the raw data. Their results can safely be interpreted in accordance with traditional statistical inference. No p-hacking was performed here.

There is a weakness to consider from merely plotting raw data and computing a few simple averages: humans are very good at coming up with compelling stories based on naive methodology. It is possible that the source of the observed variance in the data is not systematic as I previously suggested, but simply due to random fluctuations typical of weather and temperature.

Let's simulate some data to test this idea. I will set the seed to today's date. That way you know I didn't cherry pick this example. We will take the global average and standard deviation from the temperature data to simulate a random walk with gaussian innovations.

```{r}
set.seed(08182026)

innovations <- rnorm(
  n = length(1995:2025),
  mean = 0,
  sd = sd(x$temp)
)

temp <- mean(x$temp) + cumsum(innovations)

(y <- tibble(year = 1995:2025, temp = temp))
```

We'll skip ahead and just plot the raw data and moving average like before:

```{r}
y %>%
  mutate(
    lag0 = temp,
    lag1 = lag(temp),
    lag2 = lag(temp, 2),
    lead1 = lead(temp),
    lead2 = lead(temp, 2)
  ) %>%
  na.omit() %>%
  gather(,,lag0:lead2) %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  transmute(year, temp, ma_5 = mean(value)) %>%
  gather("series", "value", -year) %>%
  ggplot(aes(year, value, color = series)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1996, 2025, 4))
```

Now this is just one of infinitely many possible time series, and apparently less complex than the observed trend from before. However, if somebody told you this was a graph of the highs for May 17th over the past 30 years, they might actually believe you.

The simulated data seem to tell a story of some sort of "bubble." Something began in 1996, that started to slow down about half way to 2024. In reality, the data are completely random!

This is not to discredit the work of time series analysts worldwide. Rather, this example demonstrates the importance of providing stronger evidence before making a claim. For the temperature example, it is better to consider possible sources of variation and account for any confounding. Ideally, after doing so, the explained variation in your model would be near 100%, or at least be a reasonable amount. Without compelling evidence in the form of a well designed study, a series of carefully specified models, and accompanying model diagnostics, any model should remain under scrutiny.
